An Icon Resurfaces: The 1987 Boaterhome Is "The First Motorhome for Land and Water," Quite a Sight
37 photos
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks
The word "icon" is being thrown around a lot these days, many times without any actual weight behind it. This is not one of those times: the Boaterhome is an icon if you've ever seen one, a unique vehicle dubbed the world's first motorhome for land and water, luxurious and capable in equal measure, and a true attention magnet.
The Boaterhome is also something of an RV unicorn.
From two different producers, one in the U.S. and the other in Canada, starting with the late 1970s and through to the late 1990s, about 21 units in total were produced. Of these, several remain in various states of disrepair and even fewer are part of private collections.
Then, there's this one: the OG Boaterhome , which is also the most impeccable unit of them all, still functional, still good looking, and as luck would have it (*if you're in the market) ready for a new owner.
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks This is the Boaterhome that became Internet-famous years ago and that has made somewhat of a habit of popping up every now and then, usually when it changes hands. Whenever that happens, it never fails to make headlines, if only because the extra media attention means a better look at a rig of the kind you won't find anywhere else.
Boaterhome is ridiculous looking and ridiculously designed, but it's somehow able to avoid the trap other dual-purpose vehicles fall into. If you think of amphibious vehicles that promise you they'll conquer land and water with ease, grace, and preferably good fuel economy, they never deliver: they're neither good cars nor particularly nice boats.
Boaterhome is both, and that's because it's designed to separate once it hits a body of water. On the road and at camp, it's a nice, family-friendly motorhome with everything you need inside – like, everything, including sleeping for four, a kitchen, and a bathroom. Once you back up into a lake, it becomes a fiberglass, shallow-hull boat.
Photo: UsefulJunk/HeavyDSparks Why now? This rig is a 1987 unit, built with an '87 Ford Econoline van (E-350 series) and an '86 Sport King boat hull. Its odo currently reads a little over 15,000 miles (24,140 km), none of which were put there by the current owner.
That owner is Jason Grossman, who bought it at auction in 2022 from John Ortlieb, who had inherited it from his father, along with a lesser preserved unit. Grossman is also the owner of the Once Upon a Time in America Museum and Smoke Wagon Saloon in Kanab, Utah, which explains why the rig never got any real-life use, since it was put on display for the public.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson While here, the Boaterhome was in excellent company. The Museum also houses the Guinness-certified Midnight Rider limousine and the one-of-one Dobbertin HydroCar , but also unique or rare oddities like Hitler's head X-ray and Lincoln's hat, and a collection of 35+ cars and even more strange vehicles.
Grossman reached out to YouTuber HeavyD, aka David Sparks from the HeavyDSparks channel, to offload some inventory through consignment. Sparks agreed, on the condition that he'd be allowed to take the boat part of the Boaterhome out for a test drive, complete with the inflatable "spinning wheel of death," which Grossman agreed.
The entire test drive was documented on camera for the video at the bottom of the page, as is customary these days. Sparks himself owns a Boaterhome, though his is even rarer, being built on a Dodge chassis, longer, more powerful, but also in poorer condition – so he had a second interest in seeing how this one performed.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson The OG Boaterhome The video and the recent listing offers new insight into the rig, including extra details that were never made public before. That it could accommodate four guests, had a kitchen, and a wet bathroom was common knowledge. So was the fact that the 28-foot (8.5-meter) boat sat on a tandem-axle trailer built into the chassis of the van, or that it drew power from a Mercury Marine 200 hp DFI outboard engine.
Since the last time the Boaterhome made headlines, it's been upgraded and refreshed, to the point where its amenities are now less late-'80s-style and more modern.
Photo: YouTube / Barcroft Cars For instance, the boat section got lithium batteries, a Zantrex charger, and a 3000W inverter, as well as a new 120V AC, a new instant water heater, and a new bilge pump. Features now include a reinforced bulkhead, underwater lights, color-changing LED lights throughout, and a 22-speaker audio system.
It's been painted and re-upholstered. In terms of autonomy, it can hold 55 gallons (208 liters) of fresh water, 25 gallons (94 liters) of gray, and 25 gallons of black water, but also 27 gallons (102 liters) of fuel in a tank on the starboard side, and 35 gallons (132 liters) more in another one on the portside.
The van has also been refreshed , with new paint, new window tint, new upholstery and carpets, new fuel lines, new AC, and a new stereo, among other things.
Photo: UsedCarSite.net The listing mentions the rig is in "vintage excellent" condition, and you can tell this much from the video. Sparks himself confirms the rig runs and drives excellently, with the boat maximum out at 20 mph (32 kph) when loaded with people and gear and 31 mph (50 kph) with just him at the cockpit.
Unlike his unit, this one has a pass-through from the cab to the boat part, which means it can really function as a motorhome.
Photo: Barrett-Jackson The original Boaterhome has 18 bids as of this writing, with the listing recommending a bid range between $69,000 and $89,000. If you're not even thinking about buying it, window shopping costs nothing but half an hour of your (free) time.
